subject: On‑prem visibility egress hardening & SIEM integration — proof of approach
messages:
From: Mateo Alvarez <mateo.alvarez@redwood.com>
To: Tim Ross <tim.ross@acmefinance.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>, Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-02-01T16:12:00Z
Subject: On‑prem visibility egress hardening & SIEM integration — proposed list of constraints

Tim — thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and a small set of asks so we can lock down the architecture on our side and produce the evidence package for your audit team.

High‑level constraints we understood:
- No generic outbound internet egress from the enclave.
- All telemetry must go through your approved aggregator(s) / proxy.
- Logged artifacts must be encrypted in transit with mutually agreed cipher suites.
- Token rotation / secrets for any HEC/collector endpoints must be compatible with your rotation cadence.

Questions we need clarified to finalize the runbook:
1) Which collector endpoints will we talk to? (FQDNs + port) — Splunk HEC, internal Kafka endpoint, or S3 presigned URL endpoint?
2) Do you require an agent in the customer DMZ to forward telemetry, or can our forwarder inside the VPC push outbound to an approved proxy/egress gateway?
3) For tracing hooks: do you want Zipkin/OTLP over gRPC directly to an internal OTLP gateway, or do traces need to be batched and forwarded via your Syslog/HEC pipeline?
4) Retention/sampling: what are the retention windows for raw traces and raw logs for audit evidence?

Attachment: egress-topology-v1.pdf — very rough diagram of the three options we discussed (forwarder-in-dmz, forwarder-in-vpc+nat, batched-s3-presigned).

If you can reply with the allowed endpoints and your preference on an in‑DMZ forwarder, we’ll produce a hardened plan and a list of artifacts (keys, PKI fingerprint, sample logs) for your compliance team.

Thanks —
Mateo Alvarez
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
mateo.alvarez@redwood.com | +1 (415) 555‑0142

From: Tim Ross <tim.ross@acmefinance.com>

Cc: secops@acmefinance.com
Date: 2028-02-02T08:26:00Z
Subject: Re: On‑prem visibility egress hardening & SIEM integration — proposed list of constraints

Mateo — thanks for the follow up and the diagram (looks good). Answers inline: 

1) Allowed endpoints today (approved list):
- splunk-collector.acmefinance.internal:8088 (Splunk HEC, TLS)
- otlp-gw.acmefinance.internal:4317 (OTLP/gRPC, mTLS)
- s3-presign.acmefinance.internal (S3 proxy that hands out presigned URLs to an internal object store)

We prefer TLS/mTLS for all collection. No plaintext.

2) Preference: we prefer a forwarder in the customer DMZ (edge host) that has egress to the approved proxy pool. Reason: tight control over egress budgeting and easier audit trail. We will provide a small set of IPs that the DMZ forwarder can reach.

3) Traces: OTLP/gRPC to otlp-gw is preferred. We will accept Zipkin/HTTP as a fallback but OTLP is better.

4) Retention/sample windows: logs — 90 days raw, then indexed retention per Splunk policies. Traces — 30 days raw, 1:100 sampling for noisy endpoints unless negotiated.

Operational notes:
- We rotate HEC tokens monthly; forwarder must support token refresh via an internal secrets endpoint (we can provide a token exchange endpoint).
- We do not permit long‑lived credentials embedded in images.

I’m looping in secops — they’ll provide the IP allowlist and the token exchange API doc later today.

—Tim
Tim Ross
Head of SecOps, Acme Finance
Tim.Ross@acmefinance.com | +1 (212) 555‑0199

From: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
To: Tim Ross <tim.ross@acmefinance.com>, Mateo Alvarez <mateo.alvarez@redwood.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-02-03T11:45:00Z
Subject: Re: On‑prem visibility egress hardening & SIEM integration — proposed list of constraints

Tim / Mateo — thanks for the clarity. Sketching a concrete approach we can commit to for the DMZ forwarder option (based on Tim’s constraints):

Option A — DMZ forwarder (recommended):
- Deploy a small, hardened forwarder appliance in customer DMZ (can be container or VM).
- Forwarder collects stdout/syslog + batches OTLP traces; forwards to internal proxies listed (HEC + OTLP).
- AuthN: forwarder uses short‑lived certs issued by Acme’s internal PKI (mTLS) for otlp-gw and uses rotating HEC token fetched from your token exchange API.
- Transport: mTLS for OTLP; HTTPS for HEC.
- Egress: allowed only to the IP set you will provide. No direct wildcard internet.

Option B — In‑VPC forwarder + NAT gateway (fallback):
- Forwarder in Redwood runtime pod with NAT to egress gateway owned by Acme (still subject to allowlist).
- Requires tighter network engineering to ensure no other pods can egress.

Operational items we’ll deliver if A accepted:
- hardened forwarder image + configuration template (CIS baseline)
- sample HEC payloads and a trace sample (for your SIEM ingestion team)
- automated rotate script example hitting your token‑exchange endpoint
- acceptance test harness that validates: TLS fingerprints, HEC ingestion, trace latency under 95thp50 thresholds

I attached a rough drawio (forwarder-arch.drawio) and a small CSV with action items (matt_action_items.csv) for the kickoff.
